1:
The psalm opens with a settled confidence set against a whispered counsel of despair, and the witnesses part at once over whose voice urges the flight. The reformed John Gill fixes the ground of the trust: when David says "in the Lord put I my trust," he leans not on himself or his own strength, nor on men, princes, or armies, but on the Lord as the God of providence and of grace, and on the Messiah — the Chaldee renders it "in the Word of the Lord do I hope." Gill presses the tense: David does not say I have trusted, nor I will, but I do put my trust, a faith held fast at all times, even in the worst of times; and so he is displeased with the friends who would frighten him into flight when he has already betaken himself to the safest of refuges.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in "flee as a bird to your mountain" the double possibility that runs through the verse. It may be the serious advice of timorous well-wishers who, seeing how Saul sought his life, pressed him to some place of shelter; what grieved David was not that flight would savour of cowardice, but that it would savour of unbelief, ill becoming a saint who had so often said, in the Lord put I my trust. Or it may be taken as a taunt with which his enemies bantered him, upbraiding him with his professed confidence and scornfully bidding him see what the better he would be — "you say God is your mountain; flee to him now." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the first sense, hearing the friends urge him to some inaccessible fortress in the hill-country, and David answer that he will not act as one conscious of evil or forsaken of the Almighty, but has put his trust in the Lord and shall never be confounded. Charles Spurgeon, another puritan-evangelical voice, reads it as the craft of Satan, who, when he cannot overthrow us by presumption, seeks to ruin us by distrust, using our dearest friends to argue us out of our confidence; and David, like Nehemiah — "shall such a man as I flee?" — felt the force of it yet would not yield.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the setting and the words. Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm when Absalom's rebellion was secretly preparing but discernible, the pillars of the state shaken and the king counselled to the mountains, and hear David reject the advice with the confidence with which he began. Charles Ellicott renders the trust-clause "I find my refuge," as at Ps. 7:1, and lingers over a real difficulty in "flee ye a bird," a plural verb set beside a singular noun, which he would ease by reading "flee ye like a bird," or, with Ewald, by taking the noun for a collective — a flock startled into the hurried flap of wings the verb suggests. The reformed John Calvin, weighing the same crux, reads the disputed word as plural in its letters though singular in its points, and refers it to David and his associates, all counselled into exile; yet he will not have David flee as a sign of distrust, for though the man was often forced to hide like a poor fearful bird leaping from branch to branch, he never alienated himself from the people of God. The latin-fathers Augustine reads the whole another way, taking the mountain for Christ, called a mountain in prophecy, and hearing the psalmist refuse the heretics who cry "remove into the mountains as a sparrow," as though there were many Christs: "I keep to one mountain wherein I trust."
2:
The counsel of fear now arms itself, and the witnesses watch the ambush being laid. The reformed John Gill takes "the wicked bend their bow" for men already devising mischief and making their preparations to accomplish it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in the line more of the words of David's advisers, pressing their case: everything is ready for thy destruction, the arrow already set upon the string, and the man who hopes to despatch thee concealed in ambush — therefore flee. His fellow wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the verse the other way about, as the point where David, having directed his speech to his enemies, turns it to God and pours out his complaint before him, marking how they lay their designs for his destruction and make all things ready to execute them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the single word "privily," which, as the margin shows, preserves the image of the archer lurking in a dark corner to shoot at the upright in heart unseen. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the same clause, notes how they shoot in darkness, that the evil designed might not be seen and shunned, nor prevented by others, nor — as they vainly imagine — marked by God himself to punish it.

So a quiet difference opens over whose voice is speaking here. Clarke keeps the verse within the mouth of the frightened friends, still building the case for flight; Wesley gives it to David himself, now turned from the counsellors to lay the malice before God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch resolve it by marking the seam: the words of David's counsellors who fear for him are now ended, and David begins to justify the confidence with which he opened his song, looking past the bent bow to the throne above it. For above the earth, and above rebellious Jerusalem, is the holy temple where Jahve dwells, and in heaven the throne of the King of kings, the seat whence issues the final decision of all earthly matters (Hab. 2:20). It is the settled note of these witnesses that the archer in the dark, however ready his arrow, shoots under the eye of a God enthroned in the heavens; and whether the verse be the friends' last argument or David's first complaint, it serves in the end to set the plotting of the wicked against the all-seeing majesty that the next verses will name. The bow is bent and the arrow nocked, but the mark, the upright in heart, is one whom the Lord both sees and keeps.
3:
With the foundations themselves in question, the cry widens from David's danger to the collapse of all order. The reformed John Gill reads "if the foundations be destroyed" of a state and church thrown out of course: the laws, which are the foundations of government, despised and disregarded, judgment perverted, and the very doctrines and principles of religion derided and subverted, so that there is no standing, in a political or a religious sense. He records the Jewish readings as well — Jarchi's, which makes the foundations the priests of the Lord, the righteous who uphold the world, and points to the priests of Nob slain by Doeg; and that of Aben Ezra, Kimchi, and Ben Melech, who take the ruined foundations for the plots and snares the wicked lay for the righteous, broken not by the righteous, who can do nothing, but by the Lord who is in his holy temple. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the verse in the mouth of David's advisers and reads the foundations of truth and equity: if Saul, the vicegerent of God, has cast off all fear and regards neither truth nor justice, a righteous man has no security for his life; the priests, the preservers of knowledge, are destroyed, the divine worship overthrown, and what can the righteous man now work? John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, names the foundations plainly as piety, justice, fidelity, and mercy, the pillars of a kingdom, and hears the verse conclude that, these once torn up, the condition of all righteous men would be desperate.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gathers the philology and offers the boldest reading. By "the foundations" must be understood the principles of morality that are the foundation of society, which Symmachus and Jerome render "laws"; the image is of a house shattered by an earthquake, in which safety is not to be found (Ps. 82:5). Yet he finds "what can the righteous do?" doubtful, reporting the Septuagint and Vulgate's "since they have destroyed what thou hast established, what has the righteous done?" and preferring, by a slight change of the Hebrew letters, an emendation that yields a far better sense: "if the foundations be destroyed, what will become of the tower, or the superstructure?" The witnesses divide over the foundations themselves — whether the settled principles of law and religion, or the priests and righteous men who embody them — but they agree that the question is the last argument of despair, one that David is about to answer by lifting his eyes from the shaken earth to the unshaken throne.
4:
Against the counsel of flight David lifts his eyes to a throne no earthquake can shake, and the witnesses gather at the great turn of the psalm. The reformed John Gill weighs where "his holy temple" is to be found: not the temple at Jerusalem, which was not yet built, nor the temple of Christ's human nature, but the church, where God dwells, or best of all heaven itself, the habitation of his holiness and the true sanctuary of which the holy places made with hands were only a figure. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, opening the long meditation that carries to the psalm's end, says the shaking of a tree makes it root the deeper, so that the attempt to unsettle David's confidence only fastens him the more to his first principles. He bids the reader consider that there is a God in heaven, in his holy temple above, where, though he is out of our sight, we are not out of his; that this God governs the world from a throne of glory, of government, of judgment, and of grace (Ps. 103:19); and that he perfectly knows every man's true character, for "his eyes behold, his eyelids try" the children of men, not seeing them only but seeing through them, as the refiner knows the value of the gold when he has tried it.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the comfort of that inspection. Adam Clarke hears David say that God is still to be sought where he has set his name: though the priests be destroyed, the God they served still lives and tries the heart and reins of sinners and saints alike — "he has not promised to meet me in the mountain." John Wesley takes the temple for heaven, named as the evidence of God's glorious majesty and sovereign dominion, and the throne for the seat where he examines all causes and gives righteous sentence according to every man's works, discerning the most inward and secret actions, so that he will both reward David's innocency and discover and defeat the secret designs of his enemies.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott insists, from the parallelism, that the temple here is no earthly building but the heavenly palace of the Divine King, and finds one thought of God's supreme righteousness, high above earth's anarchy and sin, enough to reassure the psalmist. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon draws from the same throne the source of David's unflinching courage: the God of the believer is never far off, not merely the God of the mountain fastnesses but of the dangerous valleys and the battle plains, and one who pleads his precious blood in the temple above will surely defeat every device and send a sure deliverance. The witnesses do not divide: whether the temple be named heaven or the church, all read the verse as the answer to the whole temptation, that a God enthroned above the tumult sees, governs, and tries the children of men.
5:
The confidence deepens into a doctrine of God's discriminating gaze, for the same eye that tries all men tries them to a purpose. The reformed John Gill reads "the Lord trieth the righteous" as gold is tried in the fire, by afflictive providences that prove their faith and patience, their hope, their love, and their fear; and he takes the trial itself for an expression of love, since God loves his people even when he rebukes and chastens them, so that their being let fall into the hands of persecutors should not weaken their confidence in him. The trying, Gill insists, is no token of desertion but the refiner's own care for the metal he proves, so that love and chastening go together and the fire is a proof of favour, not its withdrawal. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds that God tries the children of men that he may do them good in their latter end (Deut. 8:16), and that the same holiness which makes him try the righteous makes him hate the wicked: "the wicked, and him that loveth violence, his soul hateth," for nothing is more contrary to the rectitude of his nature, and their prosperity is so far from proving his love that their abuse of it makes them the very objects of his hatred.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the second clause to its uttermost, calling "his soul hateth" an expression of uncommon strength and energy, for the violent man — the destroyer and the murderer — is one whom all the perfections of the Divine nature hold in abomination; and John Wesley keeps the balance plain, that God chastens even the righteous yet loves them and will in due time deliver them, while the wicked he hates and will severely punish. Here Henry records a dissenting turn of the verse from Dr Hammond, who would read it, "the Lord trieth the righteous and the wicked," distinguishing infallibly between them, "and he that loveth violence hateth his own soul" — that is, that persecutors bring certain ruin upon themselves (Prov. 8:36). The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, reading on into the verses that follow, take the trying of the righteous as the settled ground from which the judgment on the wicked follows as a necessity, not a mere wish. The witnesses do not divide over the love that afflicts to prove; they differ only over Hammond's reading, whether the hatred be God's toward the violent or the violent man's, in effect, toward himself.
6:
"Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and an horrible tempest" — the psalm's one stroke of terror, and the witnesses read it against the sky of Sodom. The reformed John Gill takes "the wicked" in its widest reach, of the wicked one, the man of sin, and all who worship the beast, of every persecutor and all wicked men on whom the storm shall fall. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears throughout a manifest allusion to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah: the snares are judgments that fall suddenly and unawares, the fire comes immediately from God and is inextinguishable, the brimstone is melted for their drink, and the "horrible tempest" — ruach zilaphoth, the spirit of terrors — he takes for the blast of destructions, perhaps the suffocating Arabian wind, while the portion of their cup measures out the quantum of misery appointed them (Ps. 75:8), a figure he traces even to Homer's two urns at the throne of Zeus. John Wesley reads the rain as judgments sent plentifully, swiftly, and suddenly, snares because the wicked are surprised by them and cannot escape, and understands the whole not so much of present calamities as of eternal punishments, this being their portion, the meat and drink appointed them by God.

The grammatical-historical witnesses stop over the strange figure of raining "snares." Charles Ellicott owns it an extraordinary image — snares, or nooses — and reports the emendation he thinks best, Ewald's "coals of fire" (pecham for pachim), which would yield "he causeth to rain upon wicked men coals of fire with brimstone; a glowing blast is the portion of their cup"; the "horrible tempest" he renders literally "wind of heats," a hot poisonous wind like the simoom, and hears in it one more reminiscence of Sodom stamped upon the Hebrew mind. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same word with care, judging that the shorter future affirms not a wish but a fact that follows of necessity from the verses before, and that the Hebrew for coals, in strict usage, names black coals rather than burning, so that the received text is not lightly to be mended. The witnesses do not divide over the doom — fire, brimstone, and a scorching wind for the impenitent — though they part over the one dark word, whether God rains snares upon the wicked or coals of living fire.
7:
The psalm closes where it began, in the character of God, but now the righteousness that terrified the wicked turns a gracious face upon the upright. The reformed John Gill unfolds "the righteous Lord loveth righteousness" of a God righteous in himself and in all his ways, who loves to administer righteousness in the earth — both in punishing the wicked and in maintaining the righteous cause of his people — and who is well pleased with the righteousness of his Son, satisfactory to his justice, and with his people as they are clothed with it and do righteous actions in faith, from love, and with a view to his glory, acceptable to him in Christ. He is righteous in himself and in all his works, Gill adds, and righteousness, whether it punish or save, is agreeable to his nature and his very delight. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same love as a likeness: God loves that which resembles himself, and his countenance, his very face, is ever open and unclouded to the upright, who always enjoy his salvation and know that he is pleased with them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, closing his long meditation, gathers the reason God so severely reckons with persecutors: it is because those whom they oppress are dear to him, so that whosoever touches them touches the apple of his eye. He loves the righteous and the work of his own grace in them, pleads their injured cause (Ps. 103:6), and, like a tender father, looks upon them with pleasure — "his countenance doth behold the upright" — while they, like dutiful children, are satisfied with his smiles and walk in the light of the Lord. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, turns the last clause about, preferring "the upright shall behold his countenance": by the vision of God, he says, the Hebrew poet means the triumph of right and the acknowledgment of his innocence, light and peace after darkness and trouble (Job 33:26; compare the like hope of Ps. 17:15), a hope whose highest expression is the beatitude on the pure in heart and its most glorious poetry the beatific vision of Dante. So the psalm ends on a genuine turn of the text — whether God's face beholds the upright, or the upright at last behold his face — yet on either reading the trembling trust of the opening cry is answered, and the man who would not flee is left secure under the eye, or before the face, of the God in whom he trusted.
